introduction: A teacher must first be on fire: the guide asks for a warmth that others can feel, in the face, the voice and the mere presence of a person, and treats it as the condition of all effective teaching. Its forty-two quotations are read here with forty-two from elsewhere. The image is old. A fire burns always on the altar in Leviticus; a live coal touches Isaiah’s lips; Jeremiah has fire shut up in his bones; the psalmist’s heart grows hot before he speaks; tongues of fire rest on the disciples; two travellers find their hearts burning on the road. Plato’s magnet, which passes its power from ring to ring, is the philosopher’s account of the same contagion, and Emerson says nothing great was achieved without it. The cautions are few and important. Paul knows a zeal without knowledge, James a fire in the tongue that destroys, Shelley an inspiration that no one can command, Revelation a first love that cools, and Elijah a God who is not in the fire but in a still small voice.
questions: The guide says a teacher's own state matters more than eloquence. Recall a person whose presence warmed a room: what was it in them?
Plato compares inspiration to a magnet that gives its power to each ring in a chain. What does that image suggest about how enthusiasm is passed on, and how it is lost?
Paul speaks of zeal without knowledge and James of the tongue as a fire. How can warmth be kept from becoming heat?
Shelley says inspiration comes like an inconstant wind and cannot be willed. What practices do the readings suggest for remaining enkindled?
Elijah meets God in a still small voice. How do quietness and fervour belong together in a spiritual life?

outside.why: Paul reminds Timothy to stir up the gift of God that is in him, a spirit of power, of love and of a sound mind.
Chaucer's parson gave this example to his sheep, that first he wrought and afterward he taught.
Jesus makes love among his disciples the sign by which all men shall know them.
Jesus says that he is come to send fire on the earth, and asks what he will if it be already kindled.
Paul describes the change as putting off the old man and putting on the new.
Jesus says that a man must be born of water and of the Spirit to enter the kingdom of God.
Leviticus commands that the fire shall ever be burning upon the altar: it shall never go out.
Aristotle holds that persuasion is achieved by the speaker's personal character, since we believe good men more fully and more readily.
Paul's phrase for the same state is three words long: fervent in spirit.
Micah joins the same qualities: to do justly, to love mercy and to walk humbly with thy God.
Paul writes from prison the same instruction: rejoice in the Lord always, and again I say, rejoice.
Plato's Socrates compares inspiration to a magnet which not only attracts iron rings but imparts to them the power of attracting other rings.
The Song of Solomon says that the coals of love are coals of fire, and that many waters cannot quench it.
At Pentecost the fire sits upon each of those gathered, and they begin to speak as the Spirit gives utterance.
The psalmist says that his heart was hot within him, the fire burned, and then he spoke with his tongue.
Isaiah's lips are touched with a live coal from the altar before he says, here am I; send me.
Jeremiah says that the word was in his heart as a burning fire shut up in his bones, and he could not stay.
Paul bears witness to a zeal of God that is not according to knowledge. How is a warmth that guides to be told from a warmth that misleads?
Emerson's sentence on the matter is short and absolute: nothing great was ever achieved without enthusiasm.
Paul says that without charity the most eloquent speech is sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal.
The psalm calls for a new song to the Lord, and for his salvation to be shown forth from day to day.
Jesus says that men do not light a candle to put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick, to give light to all in the house.
Proverbs knows how one person changes another: iron sharpeneth iron, so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.
Jesus likens the kingdom to leaven which a woman hid in three measures of meal, till the whole was leavened.
Jesus tells his disciples to keep their loins girded about and their lights burning.
In Acts the disciples are promised power and told they shall be witnesses unto the uttermost part of the earth.
Revelation reproaches a church that has left its first love. What keeps the fire of early days from becoming only a memory of them?
In the Qur'an Moses sees a fire afar off and goes toward it, hoping to bring back a brand or find guidance there.
James says the tongue is a fire, and asks us to behold how great a matter a little fire kindles. What distinguishes a flame that should be spread from one that should not?
The two at Emmaus ask whether their heart did not burn within them while he talked with them by the way.

Shelley says that the mind in creation is as a fading coal, which an invisible influence like an inconstant wind awakens to transitory brightness, and that no one can will it. Can a teacher be told to be enkindled?
Paul asks his friends to be blameless and harmless, shining as lights in the world.
Daniel says that they that turn many to righteousness shall shine as the stars for ever and ever.
Revelation's sharpest word is for the lukewarm, who are neither cold nor hot.
Jesus foresees a time when, because iniquity abounds, the love of many shall wax cold.
John's letter joins knowledge and love: every one that loveth is born of God and knoweth God.
Hebrews asks for reverence and godly fear, for our God is a consuming fire. Is the fire of love in these readings the same fire, and does it ask for the same reverence?
Paul's instruction to a young church is brief, and assumes the fire is already lit: quench not the Spirit.
John the Baptist foretells one who shall baptize with the Holy Ghost and with fire.
Abram is told to leave country, kindred and his father's house for a land that will be shown him.
Elijah finds that the Lord is not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but in a still small voice. What place has quietness beside all this fire?
Zechariah hears that the work is done not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit.

quran-i-see-a-fire-afar-off.text: Hath there come unto thee the story of Moses? When he saw a fire and said unto his folk: Lo! Wait! I see a fire afar off. Peradventure I may bring you a brand therefrom or may find guidance at the fire

philippians-rejoice-in-the-lord-alway.text: Rejoice in the Lord always: and again I say, Rejoice

plato-stone-of-heraclea.text: there is a divinity moving you, like that contained in the stone which Euripides calls a magnet, but which is commonly known as the stone of Heraclea. This stone not only attracts iron rings, but also imparts to them a similar power of attracting other rings; and sometimes you may see a number of pieces of iron and rings suspended from one another so as to form quite a long chain: and all of them derive their power of suspension from the original stone
plato-stone-of-heraclea.author: Plato

emerson-nothing-great-without-enthusiasm.text: Nothing great was ever achieved without enthusiasm
emerson-nothing-great-without-enthusiasm.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
